claims.text: A vanadium-rich Nb-Ta-Mo-containing refractory HEA can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
V, Nb, Ta, and Mo have favorable nuclear properties that minimize the production of long-lived radioactive isotopes.
High configurational entropy confers thermal stability on the proposed alloy.
High configurational entropy confers irradiation resistance on the proposed alloy.
The refractory HEA can be fabricated by casting or additive manufacturing.
The initial alloy is predominantly a single-phase solid solution.
Composition optimization and thermal or mechanical processing can create a fine, stable microstructure in the proposed alloy.
Fusion plasma-facing materials operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K while exposed to neutron and helium fluxes.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a nanostructured, single-phase solid solution in the proposed alloy.
Controlled nanometer-scale precipitates strengthen the alloy matrix.
Controlled nanometer-scale precipitates mitigate irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Combining low-activation refractory elements minimizes neutron-induced radioactivity.
The high-entropy single-phase structure provides intrinsic high-temperature mechanical strength.
The high-entropy single-phase structure provides intrinsic irradiation resistance.
The proposed microstructure limits helium bubble formation relative to conventional tungsten.
The proposed microstructure limits irradiation-induced defect evolution.
The engineered alloy will retain high strength and ductility at elevated temperature.
The engineered alloy will outperform tungsten-based plasma-facing components in irradiation tolerance and long-term radioactive-waste management.
Tungsten plasma-facing materials suffer helium-induced bubbles, pits, holes, blistering, and related surface degradation.
Tungsten produces higher levels of long-lived radioactive activation than the proposed alloy.

contradictions.description: The mediator is described as a single-phase solid solution while also potentially containing precipitates; precipitates ordinarily constitute an additional phase, so the overall phase-state description is internally inconsistent unless only the matrix is intended to be single phase.
